constant: Conglomerate fact-sheet dossiers — the single biggest memorisation load in this book
typicalValue: For each of ~12 Indian/Indian-operating groups: founding year, founder name, current chairman and MD/CEO names, HQ city, market capitalisation in USD billions to roughly one significant figure, annual revenue in USD billions, employee headcount to the nearest ten thousand, number of listed entities, country footprint, and the list of subsidiary companies and sectors. Magnitude bands seen: the largest Indian groups sit in the hundreds of USD billions of market cap and roughly $100-165bn revenue; large single-vertical majors in the $25-75bn market cap and $15-25bn revenue band; mid-tier and privately held groups around $2-3bn revenue.
usedFor: Answering 'why this company', 'which group company would you join and why', 'which of their strategies do you disagree with', and for grounding any GD point in a real corporate example. This replaces market-sizing constants as the quantitative memory burden for GM interviews.

constant: Corporate vision/mission statements and the named core-values list, per group
typicalValue: 4 to 7 named values per group, expected close to verbatim. Patterns include five-value sets built around integrity/excellence/unity/responsibility/pioneering; five-value sets around citizenship/professionalism/customer-first/quality/dignity of the individual; acronym-based value sets; and unusually long seven-value sets at the Europe-headquartered firms. Purpose and vision statements are one sentence and quotable.
usedFor: Explicitly required. The book instructs candidates to align every HR and ethics answer to the interviewing company's stated values, and to tie GD ethical positions to the group's founding principles. Value-misalignment is treated as a real failure mode.

constant: CSR flagship programme names per group
typicalValue: 2-5 named initiatives per group across education, community health, sustainable livelihood/skilling, women's empowerment, water conservation, and rural/village development. Skilling numbers quoted in thousands of people, village-transformation programmes in the low hundreds of villages, school-infrastructure programmes in the low hundreds of schools.
usedFor: 'Why this company' answers, and for demonstrating that a candidate has read the group's annual/sustainability reporting rather than just its Wikipedia page.

constant: Everyday Indian retail price ladders for common consumer durables and FMCG
typicalValue: Personal-care liquids in the small-bottle format priced around a low three-digit rupee figure per 100ml. Mass-market household electrical durables in the ₹2,000-5,000 band, with the premium/smart tier of the same category extending into the mid-five-figure rupee range. Candidates are expected to name the two or three genuine Indian brands that occupy each rung.
usedFor: The object-in-the-room pricing probe. This is the ONLY genuinely numeric Indian market knowledge the book tests, and it is price-point recall plus brand-ladder awareness — not derived estimation.

constant: Indian power and energy-transition structural facts
typicalValue: Coal remains the dominant generation source on cost and availability grounds; the transition is constrained by high upfront renewable capex, the intermittency of solar and wind, and the scale of investment needed in grid upgrades and storage; government policy is actively incentivising the shift; levelized cost of energy (LCOE) is the correct whole-life comparison basis between renewable options; wind carries higher maintenance burden due to moving parts while solar is lower-maintenance and incrementally scalable.
usedFor: Sector-view probes at energy, power and infrastructure employers, and the wind-vs-solar investment GD. Expected as a structured argument, not a headline.

constant: EV and mobility sector directional facts
typicalValue: Demand growth driven by environmental awareness and government incentives; high R&D, manufacturing and supply-chain capex as the entry barrier; incumbent advantage as the competitive reality; charging infrastructure and range/charge anxiety as the adoption blocker; affordable rural-facing EVs and urban compact commuter EVs named as the classic underserved beachhead segments; fuel cost inflation as the substitution driver away from ICE two-wheelers.
usedFor: EV market-entry GD and automotive GTM cases — the most frequently recurring sector in the book.

typicalValue: CASA ratio named as the primary competitive lever for a new bank — attract deposits with higher initial interest rates, then defend against switching with service quality. Macro vs micro factor framing (business cycle, recession/boom as macro; competitive intensity as micro) is expected when asked to analyse the sector.
usedFor: A live PI probe at the Tata-family process where a candidate's own mention of competition was turned into an instant sector case.

typicalValue: Monsoon performance -> crop yield -> farm income and purchasing power -> discretionary farm-equipment demand, with secondary effects on rural dealer inventory and working capital. Equipment perceived as deferrable non-essential capex under income stress.
usedFor: The agricultural-equipment demand-shock GD, and rural-demand reasoning generally. This causal chain is expected to be stated explicitly as the opening diagnosis.

typicalValue: Absence of dynamic pricing and undertrained frontline staff named as loss drivers; route-level demand shocks from regional disruption; passenger communication and real-time updates as the reputation lever; compensation and rebooking support as the containment lever.
usedFor: Airline turnaround GD and the aviation-employer PI.

constant: The prescribed Indian business-news reading diet
typicalValue: Economic Times, Mint, Business Standard as the daily Indian sources; Harvard Business Review and McKinsey Insights as the analytical sources; plus company annual reports and financial statements; plus government policy, corporate-governance and ethical-practice developments relevant to the target group.
usedFor: Stated verbatim as the preparation instruction for the Tata process. Effectively the book's definition of 'business acumen' — current-affairs fluency substitutes entirely for quantitative fluency.

typicalValue: India's population; urban/rural split; household size; number of households; income-decile or SEC bucket distribution; smartphone, two-wheeler, four-wheeler, internet or category penetration rates; per-capita consumption figures; typical sector gross or EBITDA margins; typical retail markups; working-age population; life expectancy; literacy; GDP or per-capita income. NONE of these appear anywhere in 74 pages.
usedFor: Nothing in this book. Flagging explicitly so a content build is not mis-calibrated: the standard Indian guesstimate constant set has zero presence here and must be sourced from a genuine consulting casebook instead.
